stories.title: frontend-design-skill: Free frontend design skill for Claude Code, Codex and Cursor: designs your UI on a UX Pilot canvas, then builds it in your code
stories.body:
A free agent skill that designs your UI before your agent builds it. It sends a short brief from your codebase to UX Pilot, which designs real screens on a canvas you can open and edit. Your agent then builds the screens you pick in your own stack, with your components and tokens. It works in Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and any agent that supports skills and MCP. Install

Or copy the skills/ui-design folder into your agent's skills folder (for Claude Code, ~/.claude/skills/).

Run /mcp in Claude Code and sign in. In Cursor and other agents, add the MCP server https://mcp.uxpilot.net/mcp and sign in. If you skip this, the skill walks you through it. A free UX Pilot account is enough to start. What it does • Reads your project first: product, audience, routes, colors, fonts and copy, so the brief uses your real content.

stories.title: pocket-design-mcp: Free MCP server with icons, fonts, images, components, design tokens, easings, contrast checks, SVG tools and patterns for coding agents
stories.body:
A free MCP server that gives your coding agent (Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Cursor...) a designer's toolbox: icons from 280 sets, fonts, images, components, design tokens, easings, contrast checks, SVG tools and background patterns. You ask ("put a Lucide house icon in the header", "make tokens from #4f46e5", "give this card a softer shadow") and the agent finds it and drops it into your code.

stories.title: Quoting Scott Aaronson
stories.body:
It’s now obvious that we’ll be getting, not one-off solutions to this or that complexity question, but a whole new continent of mathematical truth, one that we’d previously only glimpsed …

It’s now obvious that we’ll be getting, not one-off solutions to this or that complexity question, but a whole new continent of mathematical truth, one that we’d previously only glimpsed through fog. Picture van Leeuwenhoek first training a microscope on pondwater, or Galileo first training his telescope on the stars. That might give you some idea of how our resolution into the complexity-theoretic universe, and the whole universe of mathematical truth beyond it, has now improved.

Cogentic appears to be a specialized harness for existing LLMs to collaborate together to solve mathematical conjectures, using a central orchestrator and a shared database of intermediate proofs.

And with just that, using Gemini 4 Argon, they have already obtained a number of interesting results? Math is going through its own version of the industrial revolution.
